rows: Somewhat similar to Q2; sequential growth
Record Q2 - 16th consecutive quarter of sequential growth; growth overwhelmingly North American volume rather than pricing.

The newly announced (Aug 1) PepsiCo distribution investment agreement dominated the call: $550M convertible preferred at $75/share, expected to add ~40% incremental distribution over the next 12 months.
Management clarified the '40%' refers to distribution points, NOT a 40% topline uplift versus plan.

Gross margin fell to 38.5% (44% ex-freight) pressured by higher aluminum-can costs, ocean freight, repackaging, the flush-through of higher-cost international cans, and an unfavorable mix shift to lower-margin club.
Management reiterated sequential gross margin improvement through 2022, with Q4 margins returning to the mid-40s once international cans cycle through and the price increase rolls out.

Club channel ($30.9M Q2 revenue) is mostly reorders from Costco/Sam's, with ~175 new BJ's locations incremental; co-packers developing in-line multi-packing (vs hand-packing) to improve club margins in Q4/early Q1 2023.
Pepsi distribution transition has begun; most of the transition expected by the end of Q4; Q3 will be noisy with pipe-fill orders plus estimated product returns from terminating distributors.

Distributor termination expense will mostly be booked in Q3 within OpEx and be 'very significant' (Monster's historical comparable was ~$112M; Celsius likely higher with inflation); PepsiCo's assistance is recorded to the balance sheet and amortized as deferred revenue.
The $550M PepsiCo preferred is expected to be classified as mezzanine equity (pending finalization).
Celsius added to the S&P MidCap 400 Index (effective after the Aug 9 close), graduating from the S&P SmallCap 600.
International / Nordic weakness was supply/SKU-related (a new Sweden SKU missed the selling season) and FX; July results were strong and H2 should improve.
UK and Germany named as near-term international opportunities via the PepsiCo partnership, with ongoing UK discussions, once the US transition stabilizes.
The category decelerated to ~8% in Nielsen scan data while Celsius grew 143%-194%; new-market velocity ramps slower than mature markets.
Management to keep its 'foot on the gas' on sales and marketing in Q3; G&A and S&M leverage comes from people costs as the business scales without proportional headcount.

Pricing strategy unchanged - a phased price increase continues, monitored closely in a price-sensitive category; powder/heat-to-go sticks managed internally (not part of the Pepsi deal), gross-margin accretive.
Current orbit structure has capacity to flex up to meet the extra 40% demand in 2023 and continue expanding through 2024-2025; majority of distributor termination costs borne by Pepsi.
PepsiCo long-term revenue opportunity & gross margin progression
Updated thoughts on the Pepsi distribution agreement / long-term revenue opportunity, and how to frame the Q3 gross margin path into the mid-40s Q4 target?

Working through analysis (using the Bang relationship as reference), expects expansion into food service and independent convenience; reiterated ~40% distribution increase over 12 months; ~6% margin impact from international cans, Q3 'somewhat similar' to Q2 with sequential growth, mid-40s by end of Q4.
How much of the club strength was first-time fill-in versus reorders, and what keeps the Pepsi transition smooth?

Club expansion began with Costco (Q4) and Sam's Club (Q1); Q2 is mostly reorders, with 175 new BJ's stores incremental; transition leverages experienced team members, fills PepsiCo mixing centers first then moves to direct shipment with larger distributors.
International near-term dynamics & PepsiCo global opportunity
Will Europe weakness reverse, how quickly can Celsius move on the PepsiCo international opportunity, and what about velocity as the category slows?

Europe issues were supply/SKU-related (a Sweden SKU missed the selling season) but July was strong and H2 should improve; UK and Germany are near-term opportunities (with ongoing UK discussions) but the US transition is the priority; new-market velocity ramps slower than mature markets.
Convenience penetration, velocity & the meaning of '40%'
How is velocity factored into convenience expansion via PepsiCo, why isn't the full Bang footprint the opportunity rather than 40%, and is there a co-packing opportunity with Pepsi?

Convenience is the biggest opportunity (67% of energy category volume); new-store velocity starts slower but builds; the 40% is the internal distribution reference - explicitly clarified it is distribution, NOT a 40% topline uplift; co-packing is a down-the-road opportunity.
Nordics business & FAST protein under PepsiCo
Does the Pepsi partnership change how Celsius handles the Nordics and FAST protein business, plus cooler plans and pricing strategy?

Early in discussions but opportunities exist for the FAST protein portfolio given PepsiCo's snacks business; Celsius will enter PepsiCo's ~50,000-70,000 co-brand energy coolers and continue placing its own (2,700+ YTD); pricing strategy unchanged - a phased price increase continues.
Commentary on the heat-to-go powder sticks rollout (part of the Pepsi deal?), and S&M / G&A for the back half?

Powder product managed internally (not part of the Pepsi arrangement), gross-margin accretive, expanding into Walmart; Celsius keeps its foot on the gas on S&M in Q3, with leverage from people costs as the business scales.
Capacity for 40% expansion & distributor termination costs
How quickly can Celsius ramp capacity for the 40% expansion, and what percentage of termination agreements will Pepsi pay?

Current orbit structure has capacity to flex up for the extra 40% in 2023 and expand through 2024-2025; not all DSD transitions can complete this year (mirrors how Pepsi managed Rockstar/Bang); majority of termination costs borne by Pepsi.
Transition disruption risk & termination fee accounting
Could sales/gross margin dip ahead of the full transition benefit, and how are termination fees and the Pepsi investment accounted for?

Q3 will have 'a lot going on in the P&L' (pipe-fill orders plus estimated product returns); margins should be 'somewhat accretive' going forward (soft guidance); majority of termination expense booked in Q3 within OpEx, 'very significant' (Monster comparable ~$112M, Celsius likely higher); Pepsi's assistance recorded to the balance sheet and amortized over the agreement life; $550M preferred expected to be mezzanine equity.
